Breaking Defense reported that Trump gave the directive verbally at the UN, citing no signed executive order or formal memo, and said 'As of yet, there is no official announcement from the White House on how this is to be implemented.'

Michael Drager, a Deputy Assistant Secretary in the State Department's international organizations bureau, sent staff an email titled 'Change in Nomenclature AI to SI.' Breaking Defense noted that Trump appointees have pushed earlier terminology changes, such as 'War Department' for 'Defense Department,' and that those changes have not always gained legal status.

Only a signed executive order, proclamation or presidential memorandum counts, and it must be signed by 11:59 PM ET on Sept 30, 2026. Speeches, social media posts and polls do not count. An agency-level email such as the State Department's does not count unless it is itself a presidential action.

The National reported that the East-West pipeline had restarted and was pumping at a low rate. Its only sources were unnamed Reuters sources and satellite-data analysis. The article cited no statement from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy, the government or Aramco.

The Reuters story, headlined 'Saudi Arabia restarts East-West oil pipeline, to resume exports from Yanbu, sources say', credits the restart to unnamed sources. Aramco was trying to bring flow back to 4 million bpd, below the system's full capacity of 7 million bpd.

The Saudi-owned Asharq Al-Awsat also carried the restart under the headline 'Sources: Saudi Arabia Restarts East-West Oil Pipeline', so the report is again attributed to sources and not to an official announcement.
Sources said reaching about 40% of capacity would take a couple of days and a full restart would take 6 to 8 weeks. Another source put the full restart at up to six weeks.

Pumping has resumed at reduced rates, and tanker loadings at Yanbu appear to have restarted this week, but regular exports have not recovered. Two tankers due to load on September 23 had not loaded, and six more were scheduled for September 24–27.

Sources said volumes on the East-West pipeline were building but tanker loading at Yanbu was delayed. Reuters reported that Aramco told European refiners it first needed to build a 'critical mass' of crude at Yanbu.
Industrial Info Resources cited satellite imagery showing vessels loading crude at Yanbu after the pipeline attack.

The Ministry of Energy's statement on SPA was headlined 'East–West Pipeline Shut Down as a Precaution Following Multiple Attacks'. The ministry also posted it on X and said emergency teams were deployed to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.

Saudi Arabia shut the East-West crude pipeline after several drone attacks launched from Iraq hit it in the Riyadh and Medina regions. Satellite imagery and industry sources reported that 3 of its 11 pumping stations were damaged.

There is a precedent from April 2026. On April 9 the Ministry of Energy said attacks had cut about 700,000 bpd of East-West pipeline capacity, and around April 12 it announced on SPA that full pumping capacity of about 7 million bpd had been restored.

Argaam carried the April Ministry of Energy statement that the energy facilities and the East-West line had recovered and regained their operating capacity. The ministry has made such a restoration announcement at least once before.

The 1,200 km pipeline links the eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and has been rerouting about 4 million bpd around the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said Riyadh would hold off retaliating to give Iraq's government time to stop attacks from its territory.
The US Energy Secretary said the Saudi East-West pipeline would be back in operation within days. This came from a third party (not the Saudi government) and was about the future.

The questions resolve Yes only if official Saudi government information says the pipeline is operating now; partial capacity counts. Reports from anonymous sources or third parties, satellite data, and forward-looking statements do not count. Searches through 2026-09-27 found no Saudi official statement confirming the September restart.

On Monday, September 28, Saudi Arabia resumed crude exports through the East-West Pipeline from Yanbu, ending a 17-day export halt. The only source was Bloomberg's 'person with direct knowledge'. Saudi Aramco and the Saudi energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters reported on September 22, citing unnamed sources, that Saudi Arabia had restored operations on the East-West pipeline. The report included no official Saudi confirmation. Under the rules, claims attributed to third parties do not qualify.

A search of SPA's English site found the September shutdown statement ('East–West Pipeline Shut Down as a Precaution Following Multiple Attacks') and condemnations from other countries. It found no Ministry of Energy statement after the shutdown saying the pipeline is operating again.

The Ministry of Energy said the East–West Pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions was hit by multiple drone attacks launched from Iraq on the morning of September 10, 2026, and was shut down as a precaution. It said the attacks caused injuries and some damage that was being addressed.

Sources said Saudi Arabia restarted the East-West Pipeline on September 22 at a low pumping rate, with Aramco trying to get back to 4 million bpd. A security source said reaching 40% of capacity would take a couple of days and a full restart six to eight weeks.
On September 22, Bloomberg reported that Saudi Arabia was running tests to resume the East-West oil pipeline.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, a US official rather than a Saudi one, described the Saudi pipeline closure as a brief interruption that would last days.

In April 2026, attacks cut about 700,000 bpd of East-West pipeline capacity. The Ministry of Energy then issued an official SPA statement on April 12 saying full pumping capacity of about 7 million bpd had been restored. Precedent: the ministry has formally announced a restoration of this pipeline before.
